speaker: npc.pirate-freeholds.upriver-hist-village.npc-opening-upriver-elder
words: There is no road here. You pole downriver from the landing for a day to reach the gang camp. The port lies past the camp. Leave when the lamps go out, because you want the whole day for the poling.
variants_low: No road. Pole downriver a day to the gang camp. The port is past it.
variants_high: No road comes near Nine Bends. A day of poling downriver brings you to the gang camp, with the port past it. Leave when the lamps go out. I'll fill a water jar for your boat.

speaker: npc.pirate-freeholds.upriver-hist-village.npc-opening-upriver-elder
words: Quarrels between households come to me. Debts most of all, since the houses that stay are short of hands. They borrow from each other. I hear the same grudges every dry season.
variants_low: Quarrels and debts between the houses come to me. I hear them. That is all I do for them.
variants_high: Debts and quarrels between the households come to me. I hear each one out. Sit at my door if you've a quarrel of your own.

speaker: npc.pirate-freeholds.upriver-hist-village.npc-opening-upriver-elder
words: The roll is our only coin. The gangs downriver hire our adults on it, more each year. It pays for my guest stores: smoked fish, dry mats, fresh water. The rest of us cut reed, mend nets and dye.
variants_low: The roll brings the only coin. The gangs downriver hire our adults. More go each year.
variants_high: Our adults go downriver on the roll, more of them each year. That coin pays for the stores at my door: smoked fish, dry mats, fresh water. Eat first if you are hungry.

speaker: npc.pirate-freeholds.upriver-hist-village.npc-opening-upriver-elder
words: Go down to our landing and look at the waterline. You will find a cut mark there. The same mark is cut on all nine bends of the river. The village gave up counting the marks a generation ago.
variants_low: Go and look at the waterline by our landing. The same cut is on all nine bends. The village gave up counting the marks a generation back.

speaker: npc.pirate-freeholds.upriver-hist-village.npc-opening-upriver-elder
words: Yes, that is the cut at our landing. Its twin is on every other bend of the river. The village gave up counting the marks a generation ago.
variants_low: That is the cut at our landing. The same cut is on every bend. The village gave up counting them a generation back.

words: Alten Corimont is a river port in eastern Shadowfen, on a waterway that runs out to the sea. Argonian pirates and smugglers run the place. They take no side in anyone's war. Any crew may tie up at its docks. The dredging gangs of the lower channel are hired out of those docks.

Alten Meerhleel is a trade port and floating village north-west of Lilmoth. A harbormaster built it in the Second Era so that the swamp tribes could trade with outsiders. The tribes complained that it stood too close to the swamp. To quiet them he built a court north of the docks.

The An-Xileel are the nativist government of Argonia. They began as a party in the Oblivion Crisis that drove the Empire out of Black Marsh. They want the province free of Imperial ways. They coined the slur lukiul for Argonians who lived under those ways.

The Archeins are Argonian families who served the slavers. Under the Empire, they ran serf villages and advised the governors of the coast. Other Argonians hate them for it, because they sold their own people and worked the land for foreigners. Tribes forgive one another a great deal, but they have not forgiven this.

Archon is the eastern port and the province's legal harbour, with marsh to the north of the city and beaches to the south. Pilot families bring ships in through the estuary approach. The harbour authority's power stops at the headland.

Argonia is the name that Black Marsh took when it left the Empire, in the first years of the Fourth Era. It is a marsh country with no emperor over it. Its rulers come from inside the marsh. The An-Xileel are its government.

The Argonians are the lizard-folk who are native to Black Marsh. Their own word for themselves is Saxhleel. An Argonian hatches from an egg beside a Hist tree. The tree's sap shapes the body for life, so every tribe looks a little different. Most Argonians have a natural gift for magic and for stealth.

The Battle of Argonia was fought in the First Era, in the year 2811. It broke the last organised Argonian army. Those who lived marched into the interior and settled at Helstrom. The Emperor of that time would not send soldiers in after them.
The Blackguards are Argonian pirates and brigands of the south coast. They descend from the inmates of Blackrose Prison, the old Imperial jail. They are the largest band of criminals in Murkmire.

Blackrose is a lake city in the south, where three rivers meet. The Rose is its old Imperial prison, a day's march south of the city. Families live in the Rose now. In the old days few who entered ever left.

Blackwood is the hilly country in the west of Black Marsh. The Blackwood Road climbs through it to Cyrodiil. The people of its hills stay close to their own tree's roots and show little curiosity about strangers. They do like a riddle.

Bog iron is iron that the marsh makes by itself. Water seeps through the ground and leaves a crust of iron in the clay. The Bog Iron Workings lies below the road. The crews there cut that crust into cakes and smelt the cakes in a clay furnace.

Bones-And-Tools is a hollow deep in the jungle, under the layer of roots. It has one mouth that a creature could defend. A creature has made its lair there. It has dragged in what it took. Families who once foraged that way now live at the hiring camp, about a kilometre east. Any of them will tell a stranger why at length.
Bretic means of the Bretons. The Bretons are a human people of the west, from far beyond the marsh. To an Argonian a Breton traveller is an ojel, an outsider. The word is meant plainly.

The Bright-Throats are a tribe of Murkmire who breed horse-lizards and welcome outsiders. Their village has hatching pools and a tree-minder. They seal an alliance with a bonding ceremony and a feast. A ceremony that is called off is a break between peoples.

The Broke Column is what is left of a Legion column. When the Legion was recalled it never paid these men. Their sons and grandsons still live in a camp on a bench in the hills above the Mile House track.

The Chainbreakers are abolitionists who fight the Owing, the debt that binds a person to labour. They audit the ledgers, burn the debts they can prove false and carry the bones of the dead home, because a soul returns to its Hist.

Chasepoint is a road stage on the coast road, built by the Legion and kept now by wreck-salvage families. Salvage rights there are hereditary. The families dry recovered rope in the old stable. Two families each claim the keeper's office.

Claywater is a stop in two halves, set at one ford. The station half on one bank is built of timber and stone. The landing half across the water is mud and thatch. Each bank charges a traveller for its own half of the stop.

The College of Whispers is a society of discreet mages chartered by the Empire. They summon Daedra and raise the dead. They know more about Umbriel than any other body. The College has no hall in Argonia. A College scholar who comes looking for the dead of Umbriel is robbing graves.

The Counted Lots are the numbered pearl beds off the Archon coast. Diver families hold each lot by inheritance. The deep lots pay best and kill divers. The tally book records both the pay and the deaths.

The Cut Circle is a long stilt hall over still water at a lagoon's edge, within a day of Helstrom. One walk on piles leads in from the land. The Unbound Root, a movement that holds the Hist above every law, preaches there in the open.

The Cyrodilic Collections is a society of antiquarians from the Empire. It digs up Argonian relics, repairs them and offers to return them to the marsh. Its great hope is a museum of Argonian history in Argonia. That museum has not been built. Argonians argue over whether a find belongs in a museum or with its tribe.

The Dunmer are the dark elves of Morrowind, the land north of the marsh. House Dres, one of their great houses, grew powerful by raiding Argonians for slaves. It ran that trade for centuries. Morrowind ended slavery long ago, but the grievance on the marsh side runs two hundred years deep.

A clutch is the eggs of one family, laid together in a warm place near the roots of the Hist. The egg-tender looks after the clutch until the eggs hatch. The tender reads to the eggs, plays the flute to them and writes down each egg's parents, hatch day and star sign. A family guards its clutch because the eggs depend on the Hist beside them.
Fish-Eye Rye is a liquor from Hissmir, the pilgrimage xanmeer in southern Shadowfen. A drinker plugs the nostrils before the first swallow.

Gang Ground is the camp where the families of a dredging gang live. It stands on firm ground between the Border road and the marsh. It is about forty years old. The top terrace is dry enough for a hatching shed. The gang's clutch lies in it. The families stay because the eggs are there.

Gideon is the western frontier city, the first settlement on the Blackwood Road from Cyrodiil. Its courts still work, so an Owing made there is a paper contract that can be contested in court. Most of its people are Argonian.

Greenspring is a spring village on the way to Helstrom, where travellers stop for water and a bed. The spring water is free and can be drunk unboiled, which is rare in the region. Salt is reaching the spring. The village blames the salt works upstream.

Helstrom is the capital of the Argonian interior, a city grown into a Hist grove. The native armies withdrew there after the Battle of Argonia. The Empire chose not to besiege it. No army has ever taken the city.

Hissmir is a pilgrimage xanmeer, a stepped stone pyramid of the old Argonians, in southern Shadowfen. Outsiders and Argonians with no Hist can commune with the Hist there by passing its trials. Root Stewards run the trials and cannot refuse anyone who comes.

Hist sap is the juice of a Hist tree. The Argonians call it the tree's soul. A hatchling drinks it on the naming day. The rites of coming of age call for it again. Too much of it poisons even an Argonian. The mouth turns gold, the scales thicken like bark and visions come unasked. To an outsider it is a drug that stirs up bloodlust.
A Hist is a great tree with a mind of its own. It is older than the races of men and mer. All the Hist share one mind through their roots. Argonians hatch beside one, drink its sap and listen to it.

A Hist is a tree with a mind, older than any people. The eggs lie in a clutch near its roots. On the naming day, each hatchling drinks its sap. The sap shapes its body and scales for life. The sap is our blood and soul. When we die, the spirit goes home to its Hist. The tree-minder reads the Hist's signs and tells the tribe how the clutch fares.

House Dres was the great house of the Dunmer that built its wealth on Argonian slaves. The Dres remnant are the claimants who survived when the trade was ended. They still pursue what the house once owned in the north.

The Legion remnant is the garrisons that stayed in Black Marsh when the Empire withdrew. Their heirs count as Legion too. The Legion built the old road stages. Wreck-salvage families keep some of them now.

Imperial means of the Empire in Cyrodiil. The Empire held the coasts and the borders of Black Marsh for a long age and did not hold the deep marsh. It built the old roads, the road stages and the prisons. Then it withdrew. Its roads and stages are still here.

The League of Open Water is a body of citizens, merchants and workers who argue for civic standing that does not depend on a tribe or a Hist. They argue over citizenship and property. Its hall is in Gideon, where the courts still work.

The Lighter Flotilla is a floating quarter off the east bank of Lilmoth. Four old hulls that once carried cargo to shore now serve as houses. They lie in a line along one timber pier, with the market rafts on its far side.

Lilmoth is the southern port, built over shallow water, so large ships anchor out and small boats carry the cargo ashore. A council of merchants rules it. The flying city Umbriel destroyed it in 4E 48. It was rebuilt smaller.

Long-Water Hold is the village of a settled Naga tribe in the deep marsh. It stands on firm ground on the main poling route of the inner swamp, with a landing deep enough for loaded craft. Its people tend a Hist, villages and fields. They want the road trade. They quarrel with their tribeless kin who rob that road.

Lukiul is a slur for an assimilated Argonian, one who took on Imperial ways. The An-Xileel coined it for Argonians who lived under the Empire. An Argonian hatched outside Black Marsh cannot hear the Hist. The slur lands hardest on those.

The Many-Root Conclave is an order of Hist stewards. Its minders keep the trees. They see that each tree is asked for its consent. A minder tends one Hist and reads its signs and its will. The Conclave sends minders out to the villages.

The Marsh Charter is a tradition of fighters for hire in Argonia. The Empire's Fighters Guild charter ended with Imperial rule here. The tradition opposes taking on a foreign charter again. The work itself is old. Villages, cities and tribes hired fighters long before any guild came.

The Morrowind veterans are Dunmer soldiers from the Accession War, fought in the first years of the Fourth Era. They did not go home when the fighting ended. They stayed in the marsh and live there still.

Morrowind is the Dunmer province north of Black Marsh. Its dark elves rule it through great houses. One of them raided the marsh for slaves for centuries. Argonian armies marched into Morrowind in the first years of the Fourth Era and sacked Mournhold. Today the border is cold, quiet and resented on both sides.

Murkmire is the southern region of Black Marsh, on Oliis Bay. A dozen tribes or more live in it. No single ruler stands over them. The Naga-Kur rule the deep swamps in the north. Torchbugs light the cypress along the water. The flesh-flies thicken toward the middle.
The Murkwater are a tribe of Murkmire, hunters and trainers. Murkwater is also the name of their village, so a traveller may hear it for either.

The Naga-Kur are the Naga people who rule the inner swamps of Murkmire. They are proud, traditional warriors. They wear the bones of their fallen comrades on their arms. The villages around them fear them. They are cold to outsiders.

The Naga are a tall, adder-like breed of Argonian, seven or eight feet high, with wide mouths full of needle fangs. They live in the deep parts of the marsh. Not every Naga is a brigand. Not every Argonian hates them. The Naga-Kur rule the inner swamps. The tribeless Naga are the robbers of the roads.

A naheesh is an elder of an Argonian tribe, an office beside the tree-minder's. The naheesh carries the tribe's sacred croaks and the secrets of its naming. The people respect the elder greatly, but the office gives no power to rule.

The Night-Reed Chapter is the thieves' guild of Argonia. It is a native guild, not a copy of the one in Cyrodiil. It works the canals, the boats, the flooded districts and the rootworm routes. A new member starts as a lookout.

Nine Bends is a tribe's village built round one Hist tree on a low island, nine bends of river above the port of Alten Corimont. The water there is still fresh. The gang families of the lower channel hatched under that tree. Each year more of the village's adults are away on the downriver roll.

The Turning Path is an order of the Nisswo, the priests of Sithis. It runs the temple called the Teeth of Sithis in Murkmire. Its priests teach about change, endings and mourning. They settle quarrels between villagers.

The Nisswo are the priests of Sithis, the void god of change. They travel so that each village hears many readings of the faith. They keep no single doctrine and no central rule, so no Nisswo can settle a dispute for the whole province.

The North Cut is a road that Imperial surveyors cut north from Stormhold toward the Tear road. They abandoned it after four kilometres. It has no residents. The villagers quarry its stone for their yards. The cut now drains water onto two fields and a hamlet.

Ojel is the Argonian word for outsiders. It is a plain word and carries no insult. Lukiul is the slur that the An-Xileel coined for Argonians who hatched outside Black Marsh. Those Argonians cannot hear the Hist.

The Onkobra is a river that rises near Topal Bay and runs east past Gideon into the middle of the province. The road beside it is muddy and ill kept. The water runs white and fast near Gideon. Red Onkobra clay is a known product of the marsh.

The Owing is debt that binds a person to labour until it is paid. It is the marsh's law where there is no court. It began as a sentence of months of work, but it can now be sold and passed down, so a person can be born owing.

The Padomaic is the great ocean on the eastern coast of Black Marsh. The old Argonians say that the Hist once ruled a far larger land. That it sank into the Padomaic in the Dawn Era. Black Marsh is the small corner left standing. Archon and the north-eastern coast face the water.

The Panther Race is the river that comes down from Cyrodiil. It crosses into easternmost Blackwood and then forks by Greenspring and Helstrom. Its frogs have a chirp that musicians prize. The Pantherfish is a prized catch.

Portdun Mont is a pilots' village on the rise above a beach landing near the pearl lots. Pilot families are paid to bring ships through the approach. Their monopoly is custom and has no law behind it.

The Prison road, the Border road and the Mile House are old Imperial roads and a waystation. People still call them by their old names. The Prison road runs toward the Rose. The Tag House stands beside it on a dry rise.

The Reed-Sail Compact is the guild of boat crews, routes and ferries. It runs the boats on the rivers and the coast. Pirates called the Salt-Teeth sail inside the Compact, so a crew's name can cover a raider.

Riverwalk is a halt in a sheltered sea cove, a short way east of Thorn. It grows no food of its own. It feeds the boat crews and gives each crew a bunk. Boats tie up at a ferry stage out in the cove. A walk of planks leads there from the shore houses.

Root Talk is the council of Helstrom, a convocation of tree-minders and naheesh. It governs the city by consensus. No single voice rules. The sacred croaks that the naheesh carry are called by the same name.
The Root-Whisper are a tribe of Murkmire whose Hist withdrew after a plague. Its tree lies asleep and does not speak to the tribe. The Cyrodilic Collections helped the tribe rise again.

The Rootworm Waykeepers look after the routes of the rootworms, the great worms that carry passengers and freight through the roots. The pockets of air along them. They are a small order. Their routes are secret. A rootworm station stands at Helstrom.
The Salt-Teeth are pirates who sail inside the Reed-Sail Compact. Their boats carry the Compact's name, so a boat that looks honest may be a raider's.

The Sealed Vault is a stone undercroft beneath a ruined works. The people who found what had grown in it nailed the door shut two hundred years ago. Their note is still nailed there. A creature is shut inside. The province has bad memories of that creature.

Shadowfen is the north-western region of Black Marsh, around Stormhold. It borders Morrowind to the north and Cyrodiil to the west. It is a fetid mire of winding channels, ruined temples and Hist trees. The Legion and the Dunmer slavers have fought over it. The Great Burn started there.

A Shadowscale is an Argonian born under the sign of the Shadow. The child was taken at birth and trained to kill for Sithis. A grown Shadowscale could join the Brotherhood of assassins or leave to serve the marsh as an arbiter. A Shadowscale may not kill another Shadowscale. The order is dying out. Few remain.

Shells and Stones is a gambling game played on a marked reed mat at ferry stages. Boat crews play it through the evenings in their crews' house. They stake things on it, even the best bunk. The winner keeps the stake.

Sithis is Raj-Sithis the Changer, First Creator and Final Destroyer, the void god of change. Argonian priests teach that death and loss are its work, so a death is a change, to be mourned and then released.
Soulrest is the old Imperial capital of Black Marsh, on the south-west coast where Topal Bay meets the Southern Sea. It was the capital in the Third Era. Today the city is contested.
The Southern Sea is the water south of the marsh. Lilmoth and Soulrest are the only two cities of the province that stand on it. Oliis Bay and Topal Bay are both parts of it.

The Sul-Xan are a cult of the Naga that takes souls. They wear jade death masks and sacrifice outsiders and Argonians alike. They follow only the cruellest part of the Argonian faith and scorn the rest as weakness. Every tribe fears them.

The Sunken Archive is an order of scholars who argue over who owns knowledge. Argonians learn magic as a folk skill, with no guild of their own. So the Archive works between the local custodians of old things and the foreign mages of the Synod and the College of Whispers.

The Synod is a chartered order of mages and a rival of the College of Whispers. Both grew from the Mages Guild, which broke apart at the start of the Fourth Era. The Synod forbids necromancy and does not share what it learns freely. It has no hall in Argonia, but it hunts for artefacts of power here through buyers.

The Tag House is a shelter on the Prison road, built by the Chainbreakers to receive the bones of Argonians who die in the Rose. The Rose's families release the dead for a carriage charge, which the Chainbreakers pay and record.
Tear is a Dunmer border town on the coastal plain just north of the saltrice country. The Tear road reaches it from Thorn. House Dres ran its slave trade from Tear for centuries.
The priests of Sithis made blood offerings at the Teeth before the Duskfall. The Clutch of Nisswo still keeps the stones in repair. No sacrifices are made there now.
The Empty Cradle is the name of the order of the Shadowscales. The masters who gave it its orders are gone. Three buyers now bid for what is left of its work.

The Thorn Ash-Reed Accord is the body on the northern border that argues over title to the saltrice fields. It also argues over what the border remembers, the raids of House Dres and the grievances of the Dunmer quarter. It has a magistracy, a militia hall and a counting floor.

Thorn is the northern border city of the saltrice fields. The Tear road runs from it into Morrowind. House Dres once raided it for slaves and profited from its rice. Today the Thorn Ash-Reed Accord argues over who holds title to the fields.

A tree-minder tends a village's Hist and speaks for it. The minder reads the Hist's signs and will. It feels when the eggs or the tribe are in trouble. The Many-Root Conclave sends minders out to the villages and keeps the trees.

Naga are a tall adder-like breed of Argonian. Most of the marsh's brigands are tribeless Naga, who belong to no tribe. Many rob the tracks while merchants walk them. Cut-Rope's raiders are one band of them.

The Umbriel Witness Society is a body of people who argue over how the year 4E 48 should be remembered. Some of them want a complete record of every account. Others want a memorial place that is not disturbed. The Society has its archive in Lilmoth.
Umbriel is a flying city. In 4E 48, it came up out of the south and destroyed Lilmoth. It killed much of the south of the province.

A cutting is a piece taken from a Hist and planted away from the tree. The Unbound Root takes cuttings from a Hist. The Many-Root Conclave sees that each tree is asked for its consent. The Root takes its cuttings without asking.

The Unbound Root is a movement that puts the Hist above every law. Its people say that the Hist shape an Argonian's body and mind. That the state uses that bond to demand obedience. Some of them are victims of the state's abuse. Some are fanatics. Its preachers say that real change needs a way to sever the bond.

The Veiled Reed is the covert office of the An-Xileel, the nativist government of Argonia. It guards the province against its enemies by secrecy and coercion. Its factors travel the interior as the Reed's agents.

A xanmeer is a stepped stone pyramid built by the old Argonians. Most are ruins now. Each had a chamber for its tribe's Hist. The insides are mazes of traps and relics. Their defences still work after thousands of years.
The Xit-Xaht are a tribe of Murkmire. Their Hist directs them. The other tribes fear them. They still build in stone, as the old Argonians did.
The diggers stay out of the deep end of the seep now.
The diggers have left the deep end of the seep. The seep is being worked out. The cakes lie further from the path each season.
A giant leech has its den out past the deep end of the seep.
Leeches lie in the seep. The diggers have stopped working the deep end, where something sits in the pools. The near mud is worked out: each season's cakes are smaller and lie further from the path.
A path climbs from the bench to the road. West along the road lies the Mile House of the Eagle. Cartwright's Cross lies beyond it.
Three diggers work the season, hired from three villages. One has charge of the crew, one works the bellows, one lifts the cakes. They count the work shameful and go home when the season ends.

Cakes of iron are lifted from the mud and dried on the bank. The furnace is built new each season and broken open for the bloom. Road crews buy the iron for nails, tyres and tools. A visitor may carry off what cakes they can lift.
This is a bog iron working below the road. Iron lifts out of the seep in cakes. A clay furnace on the bench smelts it.
The column's men take a levy from the road below the camp.
The column's men take a levy from the road below the camp. Gideon's governor will not pay to clear the column. The toll company's officers want to use the column themselves.
A pardon and a wage from Gideon would end the column.
The column would disband if Gideon offered a pardon and a wage. Ask the serjeant for the column's terms.
The column's men stand a watch over the Gideon road and call the hour.
The column's men stand a watch over the Gideon road. Ask the serjeant which boats the watch counts.
The column's terms are a pardon and a wage, both from Gideon.
The watch is called every hour.
Taste the water of the pool under the Hist, then stand before it. You have leave.
You stood before the Hist and it let you hear it. The trial is answered.
The Trials of the Burnished Scales let one without a Hist commune with the Hist.

At Hissmir the Trials of the Burnished Scales let one without a Hist commune with the Hist. A Root Steward cannot refuse a comer, so I give the trial here. Ask Vees-Wai, the tree-minder, for leave to stand before the Greenspring Hist, then come back to me.
Fellrunners and marsh rats keep to the scrub around the stage.
The old capital is a short walk west. The coast road runs east to Fourth Stage. The sea lies two fields south.
Wreckage from the Southern Sea comes ashore south of the stage.
A wreck has come in on the bar. The families will not work it. Buys-Cheap has been out to look. Ask him what is aboard.
Salvage rights here pass down the families. Two families each claim the stage-keeper's office, which has carried no pay in two centuries.
Chasepoint is the last firm ground before the coast road turns inland. Past here the road needs a causeway.
A survey went out east of Soulrest to price a causeway repair. No report has come back from it. Walk the road to The Tag House on the Prison road and look for its trail.
A wrecker who pulls a person off the bar says the rescue is owed.
The wreckers who pull people off the bar keep them on as crew, to work off the cost of the rescue. Ask Opens-The-Second-Shed what that comes to.
Wreckage comes ashore south of the stage. Some of it belongs to people who think their ship is still at sea.
This week's lot came off a ship whose owners do not know it sank. The owners should be told. Ask the station-keeper who.
The Legion built the stage and stopped paying its keepers. Two families still claim the office.
No keeper here has been paid in two centuries. Two families each say the office is theirs. Each wants the arrears. Argues-With-The-Clerk speaks for one of them.
The families drag wreck timber off the south shore at low water and dry the rope in the old stable. The stall sells the past week's finds.
Chasepoint is an Imperial road stage the Legion built. The wreck-salvage families keep it now, under a reed roof on the old walls.
The landing will not mend the well in stone. That is for the well-keeper and the poler to settle.
Bog dogs hunt the banks at dawn and at dusk. A crocodile keeps to the channel.
The road runs from the ford to Cartwright's Cross, then to the Mile House of the Eagle, then to Gideon.
Imperial households live on the station bank. Argonian households live on the landing bank. Both take their quarrels to the well-keeper and the poler.
The station bank keeps the well, the counter, the beds and a stable. The landing bank keeps a plank raft that takes carts over the ford. Each bank charges a traveller for the same stop.
Claywater Station stands where the road crosses the Claywater ford. A well and a station house stand on one bank. An Argonian landing, older than the station, stands on the other.
A traveller pays at the well and pays again at the landing. Each half says the stop is its own.
The well and the landing each charge a traveller for the same stop. Ask the poler across the ford what the landing wants for its half.
Living people leave the Rose on the papers of the dead. Every name is written in the charge book in the keeper's hut.
A trafficker moves living people out of the Rose on the papers of the dead. Every charge is written in the keeper's book, in his hut. Read it.
That pearl came off the deep lot. Its worth fixes the share the heirs are owed. The claim is settled in Archon.

The Blackrose Chainbreakers audit the Owing and burn false debts. They hold that freeing debtors and carrying the dead home are one work, because a debtor who dies far from the Hist may never get home.

The Many-Root Conclave is the order of stewards who care for the Hist. The Conclave sends tree-minders to the villages. A minder tends one tree and reads its signs. Each minder sees that the tree is asked for its consent. A minder feels when the eggs are in trouble.

The Reed-Sail Compact is the guild of boat crews. It fixes each crew's share of a route and holds its monopoly by stoppage. When a council tried to license the boats that carry cargo ashore from anchored ships, the crews stopped work for two weeks.
I keep out of the business of the orders and companies.
That is past what I know of this place.
Many newcomers ask that. I am no teacher.
Folk are folk. Ask them yourself.
I have heard nothing of that.
I have not been that far.
That is not my trade.
I have heard nothing worth repeating.
I cannot help you with that.
Some cargo on this flotilla is written in the speaker's book and nowhere else.
The speaker keeps a tally of cargo off a hull that never reached the quay. Bring me that tally. Take it unseen.
The council wants lightering licensed. The crews want the tariff opened.
The council wants every lighter licensed. The last time it tried, we stopped the port for two weeks. Ask Xal-Jei what the crews would take. Then carry it to the council.
Every cargo in the bay comes ashore in a lighter's hold. Not all of it goes over the quay.
Some cargo comes ashore at night and never touches the quay. It is settled at the dice tables. Ask Reeh-Tei what comes past the nets.
That is the tally. Give it here.
Salt is reaching the spring from upstream. The village blames the salt works. The Hist over the spring has begun to sicken. Giant wasps nest near the huts.
Helstrom lies south-west, past Ux-Aneet and Cut-and-Carried. The road and the river landing are each a short walk from the spring.
So the households have spoken. The body came out of the water we all drink, and that will be said aloud now.
A body lay in the spring water. Some at the spring would rather it was not spoken of.

We lifted a body out of the spring. The whole interior drinks that water without boiling it. Two households at the spring do not want the body mentioned. Ask Mee-Sei and Tsono-Ra what they saw, then come back to me.
The tree-minder tends the Hist and the spring-keeper keeps the spring. The root-herald trades for the tribe. The spring families cook, fetch water and mend rope.
Salt is reaching the spring. The village blames the salt works upstream. The answer lies under the roots, in the drowned galleries.
Our Hist has begun to sicken. The village blames salt from the works upstream. Ask Im-Moro, who keeps the spring, what the water tells her.
The water costs nothing here. The tribe has always given it free.

Two convocation delegations sleep in my beds. They do not pay pitch rent at Nine-Trunks. They want the use of the spring written down before the next convocation. Ask the spring-keeper, Im-Moro, on what terms the spring is kept.
The tribe serves travellers bound for Helstrom. Water from the spring is free. Beds and rope cost a great deal.
The water is free to anyone who comes. Beds and rope are paid for. That is how it will be set down for the convocation at Nine-Trunks.
Greenspring is a Hist village beside the fork of the Panther Race. The tribe's Hist grows over a spring of clean water.
Hearth Heal is a small mending that closes cuts and eases bruises. The spring-keeper teaches it for a price.
Salt is reaching this spring from upstream. Ask in Helstrom about theirs.
The city spring at Helstrom runs sour on a cycle. The assembly will not time it in open session. The spring-keeper here, Im-Moro, keeps clean water. Ask her how she tells when water is turning.
A naming needs the Hist and its hatchery pool. The camp that keeps the clutch is a day downriver.
The refuge downriver has a clutch to name and no Hist of its own. The village has offered to do the naming. Ask the elder.

The talk at the Greenspring lodge is that more cult couriers and sap-tappers are passing through on the way to Helstrom than anyone remembers. The lodge-keeper swears a few of the quiet ones are Veiled Reed factors, the covert agents of the An-Xileel, keeping an eye on who comes and goes.

Travellers through Greenspring say that cutters have been working at the edge of a Hist grove inland. A grove is a stand of the great trees that have minds. The minders of the Conclave keep such trees.
Salt is reaching the Greenspring spring from the salt works upstream. The village blames the works for it. At the lodge, the other talk is of who will carry the next load to Helstrom.

Travellers through Greenspring say that a Hist in the south has gone silent. That means the tree has stopped speaking to its tribe. A Hist can fall silent when it is sick or when it shuts itself off from the other Hist.
Talk in the gang's camp is that more adults go downriver on the roll each year. The roll is the list of debtors in the dredging gang. It is read out on the barge, never in the camp.

The Mile House says a pardon and a wage may come from Gideon for the men of the column. The same talk says the governor will not pay to clear the camp. It also says the toll company would sooner hire the men than pay them off.
Slaughterfish and osheeja gar hunt the water under the hulls.
A landing stage runs from the pier foot to the Lilmoth track. Boats leave the pier for the anchorage and for Archon.

The lighter crews live aboard their hulls. The Reed-Sail Compact holds the posts of speaker, lighter's master and purser. The council once tried to license lightering. The crews stopped the port for two weeks.
Large ships cannot dock at Lilmoth, so they anchor out in deep water. The lighter crews carry every cargo from the anchorage to the quay. Their moorings lie outside the tariff line.
The Lighter Flotilla is four working hulls moored as houses along one timber pier off Lilmoth's east bank. Market rafts lie along the other side of the pier. A trade ship lies at its head.
Tags for people still alive hang on the Tag House wall. The names on them belong to families in Vaunting.
Some of the tags on my wall are hung for people who are still alive. I did not hang them. Sal-Ozzu waits under the shelter. Ask her whose names they carry.
A diver drowned on lot four. It was never hers. Lots pass by inheritance. Disputes over them are settled in Archon.
A diver came up dead on lot four. She had no right to work that lot. Ohl-Jei dives beside it. Ask him.

The camp's nagas rarely kill a walker on the track, since his tribe would come for the camp, so they take cargo instead. Cut-Rope's raiders work the same tracks. A crocodile, death hoppers and hackwings den round the pond.
The camp's path leaves the track at a cane gate between two totems. The track runs on to the Polers' Camp. Guides there pole travellers to Dead-Water Village.
Six live at the camp. The lieutenant cuts the receipts. A band of five keeps the gate, the fire and the bend in turns and sleeps in the hide tent.

The camp's nagas stop walkers on the track and relieve them of cargo, then let them go. For every load, the lieutenant cuts a notched tally stick and hands it over as a receipt. The nagas smoke hides over the fire. They set the best aside for trade.
The North Cut Camp is a raiders' camp on a bench above a pond, where the walked track bends. Walkers come into view below it before they can see the camp.
Beds here cost a great deal, but the delegations still pay for them. They do not pay the pitch rent at Nine-Trunks.
Nine-Trunks rents convocation pitch at a high rate. Two delegations lodge here. Ask Haj-Tei what they pay for his beds, then take the matter to Nine-Trunks.
Both claims are old enough that each side can argue its case: our traps, and the port's right to load there.
The village's fish traps stand where the free port's boats now load. Ask the elder whether the village will argue for them.
The camp's men take payment each season to keep the track quiet.
The men of the North Cut Camp take payment each season to keep the track quiet. Long-Water Hold has begun paying it.
The camp's men cut a tally-stick as a receipt for each payment.
Little hunts the slope. Slugs, gar and torchbugs keep to the shallows and the reeds. The danger is the debt, which grows with every broken tool.

The way up leads from the hatching shed to the Border road. The way down leads to the landing and the barge pier. The gang walk runs to Alten Corimont. A root route climbs out along the two Hist roots on the west bank.
The families of the hands on the roll live here, Argonian and Khajiit. A clutch-keeper tends the shed. Two overseers keep the gang's debts for the house that holds the camp.

The gang works the free port's channel from the barge below the camp. Its names and debts are read from the roll at the top of every shift. The families keep the camp, the water and the hatching shed.

Gang Ground is the camp of the dredging gang's families. It stands on a slope of firm ground between the Border road and the marsh. A warm hatching shed on the top terrace holds the gang's egg clutch.
The deep lots drown divers. Gar fish school over the beds. Swamp jellies drift among the buoys.
The lots lie off a low sand spit. The beach landing below Portdun Mont is west along the shore. Archon lies beyond it.
Diver families from Archon hold the lots by inheritance and share the tenders. A tally book records the takings and the drownings.
Divers work the lots from tenders moored above them. The beds lie three to four fathoms down. The deep lots pay best and drown the most divers.
The Counted Lots are pearl beds inside an offshore bar east of Archon. Buoys mark each numbered lot.
The bone-tag came back from the villages. We were told she walked out of the Rose. If a tag comes back, there are bones behind it.
A bone-tag came back to me from the villages, for a woman of the Rose. Her family were told she walked out years ago. Vees-Kai of that family waits under the shelter. Take her the tag.
The toll is argued over every night. Last night it ended in an accusation.
The toll is argued over every night. Last night the argument ended in an accusation. Ask the toll-holder about it.
The cove is the only sheltered water on this coast. If it silted up, the boats would put in elsewhere. The way across the cove is sounded every morning.
Thorn is a short walk away by the Tear road. Canoes leave the ferry stage for Hissmir, Murkwater and the Tide Fair.
A household of herb-gatherers keeps the long house. Boat crews sleep in the crews' house on the spit. The toll-holder and two toll hands keep the toll post.
The cove silted up in one night. Boats will pass Riverwalk by if it stays silted.
The way across the cove silted up overnight. Boats will pass Riverwalk by if it stays silted. Ask the stage-mistress about it.
The way across the cove to the ferry stage is sounded every morning.
The people of Riverwalk earn their living from the ferry stage and the toll on the boats.
Thorn and Hissmir each claim the toll. Paying either one counts as taking that side.
Thorn and Hissmir each claim the toll on the pilgrim water. Paying either one counts as taking that side. Ask the stage-mistress what she makes of the two claims.
The village lives on the ferry stage and on the toll on boats entering the pilgrim water. The crews are fed and lodged here, since the village grows no food.
This is a halt in a sheltered sea cove at the mouth of the pilgrim water. A plank walk runs from the shore houses across the cove to the ferry stage.

The band works in turns, so the camp is never left unwatched. One stands at the gate totems. One watches the bend and whistles when a walker comes into view, while another smokes hides at the fire as the rest sleep.
The roll is the list of hands who owe the house. It is read on the barge. A witness knows every family and every name on it. When a thing is done in the camp, the witness can say who saw it.

The lodge is the village inn, where travellers bound for Helstrom sleep. A bed costs one price a night that the village agreed together. Rope is sold there too. Water is free, so beds and rope pay for everything else.

A boat crew poles and loads the boat along the channel to the stage. The crew sleeps at the landing the boat reaches by dark. Riverwalk grows no food of its own, so it feeds each crew and gives it a bunk.

The lieutenant gives the camp's orders. The load is taken and the walker goes free with a notched stick as his receipt. A walker is never killed, because his tribe would then come for the camp. A robbed walker comes back next season.

The carrier takes the dead from the Rose home to the villages. The Rose releases a body. The Chainbreakers pay the charge. Then the carrier wraps it and carries it away. Bones brought to the dirt near a tree can still go home.

The column was a body of Legion soldiers on the border road when the Legion was recalled, about two centuries ago. Their pay was owed. Part of the column did not march home. The Legion never paid them.

Bog iron forms in stagnant water rich in iron. A digger lifts it from the seep in cakes. Each season a new furnace is built, then broken open for the bloom. Each digger goes home to a different village when the season ends.

A lot is a numbered stretch of seabed that passes down one diver family. No other may dive it. The lot diver fills a net with shells and grades them by size before any opens. The tally book records takings and drownings alike.
A dyer buys cut reed by the armful from the cutters along the bank, then steeps it in the vat until the colour takes. The dye stains the dyer's hands, wrist and all. The stain shows the trade.

The flotilla speaker speaks for the lighter crews when the Lilmoth council writes. The speaker calls the crews to a vote on the answer. No hull casts off without the speaker's nod. Once the crews voted to stop the port for two weeks.
A gang is a crew of hands who owe money to House Dres. A hand dredges the channel off the barge and sleeps on land with the family. Food adds to the debt, and so do sickness and broken tools.

Households whose adults are all downriver on the roll keep the village going. They keep the trade-house and the smokehouse running. They keep a kin-house swept for whoever comes back. More adults go downriver every year. Fewer return.

Helstrom is the capital of the Argonian interior. It lies south-west of the spring, past the village of Ux-Aneet. Travellers bound for it stop here for water and a bed. The spring water can be drunk unboiled, which is rare in this region.
A clutch is a family's eggs. The clutch-keeper tends them until they hatch. The keeper keeps the hatching shed's fire low and the nest dry. Dry reed for the nest comes from the basket by the door.

The spring is a clear pool under the Hist, ringed by boulders. The spring-keeper holds the ladle on its cord at the stone lip. Water is free to any traveller. Visitors are expected to taste it before they speak.
The nisswo of the Teeth meets pilgrims where the way meets the water and asks what offering they bring. Nisswo are Argonian priests of Sithis. A pilgrim who comes empty-handed is turned back.

The Rose is the old prison south of Blackrose. Families born there three generations deep live in it now and will not call it a prison. The carriage charge on its dead is the most resented coin in the south.

A lighter is a boat that meets deep-water ships and takes their cargo ashore, so every cargo in the bay comes ashore in a lighter's hold. The master casts off the Lilmoth lighter and carries passengers between the city pier and the anchorage.

Large ships cannot dock at Lilmoth, so lighter crews carry their cargo ashore. A lighter hand hauls cargo from the anchorage into the lighter's hold, bails between runs and sleeps in a bunk below the foredeck.

A long house holds a household and its guests under one roof. The long house at Riverwalk stands on piles in the shallows. Its family has kept it a long time. Reed mattresses are aired every dry morning.

The tree-minder tends the village Hist, the great tree with a mind of its own. The minder clears the fallen leaves from its root each dusk. The Many-Root Conclave, an order of Hist stewards, sent the village that office.
A net-mender is a hand who sits with torn nets and worn gear and makes them sound again. The work is done in the open, where anyone can watch the mending. Anyone may bring a net.
Two overseers keep the gang's debts for House Dres, the old slaving house. One sits by the fire with the ledger. The other walks the yard at dusk and checks each door.
A walker can wade the ford, but a cart cannot. The poler takes carts over on a plank raft and charges by the wheel. A cart that crosses without paying the poler breaks the landing's oldest rule.

A priest of the Teeth rings the bell that the pilgrims hear from the landing. The priests hold the bell and the teaching. The band below them holds the stair. The nisswo meets each pilgrim and asks for the offering.

The purser is the officer who keeps a trade ship's books and counts what comes aboard and what goes out. The purser sells the ship's goods untaxed and lets bunks below deck to anyone who pays the fare.
Reed is cut along the bank by the reed cutter and tied in bundles so it can be carried. It is sold by the armful to the dyer and to anyone who is building a house.

This is the Blackwood Road, the Imperial road that carries carts between Leyawiin and Gideon. Travellers pass the Mile House of the Eagle and Cartwright's Cross on the way. It closes in the monsoon season.

A root-herald is a tribe's envoy to the outside world. The herald gathers news and bargains over trade. The office is the tribe's own and holds no rank in the state. Greenspring's herald keeps a ledger of goods sent down the road to Helstrom.

Wreckage from the Southern Sea comes ashore on the coast south of the stage. The families hold hereditary salvage rights and guard each stretch of shore. Taking timber from another family's stretch is forbidden.

The scrubber carries a bucket up from the landing and cleans the teeth down to the waterline. The scrubbing is a ritual, so nothing is repaired or added. Touching the stone beneath the waterline is forbidden.
The stall sells the past week's salvage. Each lot is counted at the stall and sold under the name of its ship, read off the bow-board. A lot without its ship's name does not sell.

The serjeant keeps the column's watch, called on the hour day and night. He writes the duty roster in his own hand. The pay book still holds the column's last entry. He parleys with a stranger before he fights.
A smith works iron at the forge and mends the household tools of a settlement. Bog iron, smelted into a bloom, is the raw metal such a forge works. The smith is paid in coin or in kind.

The spring families live around the spring. They cook at the fire stands and fill the lodge jars. They mend rope to sell. When two families quarrel, the tree-minder hears both sides out and settles it.
Boats moor at the stage. Passengers pay their fares on the stage before boarding. The stage calls each crew by the name of its boat. A passenger stays a traveller until the village has fed them.
Chasepoint is an Imperial stage. The stage-keeper's office is inherited. No keeper has been paid since the coast road stopped being kept. Two families each claim the office. Neither gives way.
The surface tender is the one who stays in the boat and minds the divers' lines from above. The tender never enters the water. The diver families share the tenders moored over the lots.

The tag-keeper hangs a tag on every basket and writes each carriage charge in the book before a bundle is wrapped. A body leaves the Rose's hands only under the shelter, never on the road. It never goes without its tag.
The band at the Teeth keeps the watch on the stair, carries the offerings in and stands in the shallows through each rite. The shallows are cold. This work is the temple's whole daily rite.
The toll is a levy on each boat that enters the pilgrim water, written on a slate and paid at the toll post. Thorn and Hissmir each claim it, so the slate has one column for each.
Claywater is two halves at one ford. Each bank charges a traveller for its own half. The station half is built of timber and stone, the landing half of mud and thatch. The station well is cracking.

The elder keeps the guest stores by the door and houses strangers under the elder's roof. Quarrels and debts between households are brought to the elder. The elder sees that the offerings at the foot of the tree stay filled.
The station well is Imperial-built stone, drawn by a windlass at set hours. It is failing, because its stone is cracking. A traveller asks the well-keeper before drawing any water.
Death hoppers hunt the wet ground below the rise. A wisp comes out after dark.
The Prison road runs past the rise. The Rose lies one way along it. The villages lie the other way.
A Chainbreaker tag-keeper keeps the hut beside the shelter. A carrier from the villages wraps the dead. A family from the Rose waits in the doorway until the charge is paid.
The Rose's families release a body here for a carriage charge. The Chainbreakers pay the charge and write every payment in a book. The carrier wraps the bundle for the road.
This is a handover shelter on a dry rise beside the Prison road. The Rose's families bring their dead here. The villages' carrier takes them home.
Tag 17 was released after a week. No name was given. The Chainbreakers paid the forty drakes. The Rose is where to ask whose bones those were.
Some faction claims to have found the temple's lost first purpose. The Clutch accept that the purpose is lost. They teach the loss to pilgrims.
A voriplasm lies in the flooded deep room and strips anything that falls into the water there. Leeches and swamp jellies keep to the shallows.
Fourth Stage, the old road stage, lies a short walk north of the temple.
Priests of the Clutch keep the temple, with a band of four under them. They take an outsider in for the right offering.
The Clutch scrub the black stone teeth clean down to the waterline as a rite. They make no repair and add nothing.
The Teeth of Sithis is the largest Sithis temple in Murkmire. The Clutch of Nisswo still tends it, though the purpose it was built for is lost.
Outsiders go into the Teeth only with the right offering.
Outsiders go into the Teeth only with the right offering. The nisswo meets each pilgrim and asks what offering they bring.
Hackwings nest on the hill above the camp. Marsh rats come out at night.
The track runs down from the camp to the Mile House of the Eagle and to Cartwright's Cross. Both stand on the Gideon road.
Six names are on the duty roster: the serjeant and five descendants of the column. Their forebears were levied from every province. They wear the Legion colours as an inheritance.
The men keep watches, called on the hour. They take money from every traveller on the track and call it a levy. The levy buys their food.

The Broke Column is a camp of four Legion tents on a level bench in the hills above the Mile House track. A spring tarn lies behind it. The men there are the sons and grandsons of a column that the Legion left unpaid when it was recalled.
Creatures live in the pond below the bank. Scorch marks cover the shelf, and the offerings nearest the water are the most burnt. A dry crackle sounds here with no flame behind it.
The Tear road stage is the way to and from the shelf.
A headwoman from one of the villages is at the shelf. Asked why, she says it is her village's turn. The older villagers are embarrassed that the offerings are now tools and salt.
Four villages send offerings to the shelf each wet season, in rotation. Tools and salt lie on it now. The offerings have become more practical over the years.
This is a stone shelf on a bank above a black pond. Villagers leave offerings on it for Haynekhtnamet, a wamasu said to live in the water, to hold back the seasonal flooding.
The heirless lot must be valued before anyone claims it. The drowned diver's basket lies eight metres down by the fourth lot.

A lot has outlived its last heir. Four families dive it to stake a claim. Anyone who takes it must pay a share of its worth to the heirs' line, so the lot must be valued first. A drowned diver's basket lies on the deep lot by the fourth lot, eight metres down. Bring me what is in it.
River predators lurk on the approach below the village. Swamp jellies drift in the shallows by the landing. A moon adder keeps to the bank.
The gang camp is a day's poling downriver. The port lies beyond it. No road comes within sight of the village.
Every year more of the village's adults are on the downriver roll. The tree shows the strain. The households left behind are short of hands. The elder settles their quarrels and debts.

No income reaches the village but its own people, hired out downriver on the roll to the gangs of the lower channel. Those who stay cut reed, mend nets, smoke fish and dye. They also keep the trade-house and the hatchery.

Nine Bends is a tribe's village built round one tree, nine bends of river above the port. The water there is still fresh enough to drink. The gang families of the lower channel were hatched under the tree. Their camp a day downriver has no claim on it.
The old offerings corrode where they lie. The salt goes on the shelf with them.
Four villages bring offerings here each wet season, in turn. Salt and tools, these days.
Four villages bring offerings here each wet season. This year is my turn. The flooding got worse. Coin is no use on that shelf. Bring me river salt to lay on it.
That is the cut mark at the landing. The village stopped counting them a generation ago.
The same cut mark shows at the waterline on each of the nine bends. The village stopped counting them a generation ago.
The same cut mark shows at the waterline on each of the nine bends. One is at our landing. Go and look at it.
The graves at White Rose lie far from any Hist. The Chainbreakers carry such bones home, but the carrying starts at White Rose.
White Rose Prison holds the graves of our people. They died mid-Owing, far from their Hist. The Chainbreakers carry bones home. Okan-Sei carries for the villages. Ask him.
